prompt: What does `=ROWS(A:A)` return in a current Excel workbook?
hint: The number of rows every sheet has.

prompt: A CSV of 1,200,000 lines is opened in Excel, the warning is clicked away, and the file is saved again as CSV. What does the file hold now?
hint: What did the sheet hold when it was saved?

choices.text: Only the first 1,048,576 lines
choices.why: Right. Saving writes back the rows that arrived, and the other 151,424 no longer exist anywhere in the file.

choices.text: All 1,200,000 lines, because Excel kept the rest in a hidden second sheet
choices.why: Excel does not move the overflow anywhere. The lines past the last row are simply not loaded.

choices.text: All the lines, since saving writes the original file back unchanged
choices.why: Saving writes what the sheet holds, and the sheet never held the last 151,424 lines.

choices.text: Nothing new: Excel refuses to save a file that it did not load completely
choices.why: It saves without complaint. That is why the loss can become permanent.

prompt: A CSV has 1,200,000 lines, header included. How many of its lines does a current Excel sheet leave behind?
hint: The sheet's rows against the file's lines.

prompt: Why can a template made long ago still stop at 65,536 rows when a current Excel opens it?
hint: Whose limit is it: the program's or the file's?

choices.text: A current Excel caps every sheet at 65,536 rows unless the data model is switched on
choices.why: A current sheet has 1,048,576 rows whether or not a model exists.

choices.text: Templates are given fewer rows than workbooks, to keep them small
choices.why: A template in the current format has the same grid as any workbook.

choices.text: It is saved in the `.xls` format, and the limit belongs to the format
choices.why: Right. Excel still opens and writes .xls, and a file in it keeps the old grid whatever version opens it.

choices.text: A CSV file can hold at most 65,536 lines, so the data never arrives in full
choices.why: A CSV has no row limit at all. The limit is in whatever receives it.

prompt: An analyst has to summarise five million rows of sales by month. Staying in Excel, what does the lesson point to?
hint: Which part of Excel has no grid of rows?

choices.text: Split the rows across five sheets of a million each
choices.why: Every formula and every pivot would then have to span five ranges, and one forgotten sheet is a wrong total.

choices.text: Load them with Power Query into the data model, whose limit is memory
choices.why: Right. The model holds columns compressed and a pivot table can summarise rows no sheet could hold.

choices.text: Save the workbook in the `.xls` format to make room
choices.why: That format has fewer rows, 65,536, not more.

choices.text: Lay the rows out across the 16,384 columns instead of down the rows
choices.why: Five million records across columns breaks one row per record, and still does not fit.

prompt: Sale `S1105` shows a price of 96. What does the cell itself record about that value?
hint: Ask what the cell would tell you three months later.

choices.text: The value, and the name of whoever typed it last
choices.why: A cell holds a value. Show Changes, on a co-authored file, keeps a list of recent edits beside it; the cell does not.

choices.text: The value and every earlier value, as long as the file was saved
choices.why: Saving replaces the value. Earlier ones survive only in whole earlier versions of the file, if any were kept.

choices.text: The value and the date and time it was typed
choices.why: No date is stored with a typed value. Nothing in the cell says when it changed.

choices.text: Only the value: not who typed it, nor when, nor why
choices.why: Right. Whether 96 is a discount or a slip for 106, the cell is the same cell.

prompt: Co-authoring on OneDrive or SharePoint removes the e-mailed copies. Which of these does it still not give?
hint: It fixes the number of files. What about the data in them?

choices.text: One file that everybody opens and edits at the same time
choices.why: That is exactly what co-authoring gives.

choices.text: A rule that holds even against a paste
choices.why: Right. Validation is still advice a paste ignores; a database's constraints are not.

choices.text: Earlier versions of the whole file, ready to restore
choices.why: Version History keeps those. The catch is that a version is the whole file, not one edit.

choices.text: A list of recent edits, cell by cell, with who made each one
choices.why: Show Changes lists those. What it does not record is why.

prompt: Which of these does a database do that a workbook does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of rules, of many writers, and of history.

choices.text: Refuses a row that breaks a rule, whoever sends it
choices.why: Right. A price that is not a number, or a sale naming a product that does not exist, never gets in.

choices.text: Shows the data as charts with slicers
choices.why: That is a reading job, and Excel does it well. A database holds the records.

choices.text: Lets many people and programs write at once, each change complete or not at all
choices.why: Right. That is what lets a web shop and a counter write sales at the same moment.

choices.text: Makes every number correct, whatever is typed
choices.why: It refuses what breaks a rule. A wrong price that obeys every rule still gets in.

choices.text: Records who changed what by itself, instead of relying on people to note it
choices.why: Right. The history is kept by the system, not by memory.

prompt: Put the week of the e-mailed workbook in the order the lesson tells it.
hint: From one file to two, and then to somebody's afternoon.
items: The owner e-mails cafe-serra.xlsx to the employee
The owner adds two wholesale sales to her copy
The employee changes the price of S1105 in his copy
Two files with one name, each missing a change
trap: Merging is the last step because it is the cost of all the others; nothing earlier in the week warns that it is coming.

prompt: Match each public case to its mechanism, as the lesson states it.
hint: Each one is a mistake this course has already named.

pairs.right: Rows past the old .xls limit never arrived
An average whose range left out five countries
Spreadsheets filled by copy and paste, and a sum where an average was meant
Text converted into dates on the way in

prompt: Which lesson of this course answers the Reinhart and Rogoff mechanism most directly?
hint: The range was typed once and never grew.

choices.text: Lesson 6, which repairs dates and numbers stored as text
choices.why: That answers the gene-name case: a value typed by whatever opened it.

choices.text: Lesson 7, whose tables make a formula read every row of a column
choices.why: Right. A structured reference takes in rows added after the formula was written.

choices.text: Lesson 13, which loads files with Power Query
choices.why: That answers the copy-and-paste case and the row limit, not a range that missed rows.

choices.text: Lesson 9, whose conditional formatting highlights the odd value
choices.why: Nothing about the five missing countries looked odd. They were simply outside the range.

prompt: By the lesson's argument, what would have shown the Public Health England gap on its first day?
hint: The lesson points back to the checks of lesson 1.

choices.text: Saving the templates more often
choices.why: Saving more often keeps the truncated rows more often. The rows were never in the template.

choices.text: Formatting positive results in red so they stood out
choices.why: The missing results were not in the sheet to be coloured.

choices.text: Protecting the template sheets with a password
choices.why: Protection stops typing over cells. It does nothing about rows that never arrive.

choices.text: Counting rows in against rows out
choices.why: Right. The same kind of check as lesson 1's counts after a paste.

prompt: In the London Whale case, what part did the spreadsheet play, as the lesson states it?
hint: The task force separated the cause of the losses from what hid them.

choices.text: It made the risk look smaller than it was
choices.why: Right. The trades caused the losses; a formula divided by a sum where it meant an average, in a model fed by hand.

choices.text: It caused the losses by placing trades on its own
choices.why: Spreadsheets did not trade. People did, and the model measured the risk of what they held.

choices.text: None: the task force found no problem with the spreadsheets
choices.why: Its report named the copying and pasting and the wrong denominator.

choices.text: It counted the profits twice, which hid the losses
choices.why: The error was in measuring risk, not in counting profits.

prompt: Typed into a cell, the gene name `SEPT2` is read by Excel as a ___.
hint: The 2nd of September.

prompt: How does the lesson split the signals between the two destinations?
hint: One kind of problem is about putting data in; the other about getting answers out.

choices.text: Problems with reading point at a database; problems with writing at a BI platform
choices.why: The other way round. Many writers, rules and history are a database's job.

choices.text: Problems with writing point at a database; problems with reading at a BI platform
choices.why: Right. Café Serra could need either one without the other.

choices.text: Every signal points at a bigger computer running Excel
choices.why: More memory helps the model, but no computer gives a file many safe writers or one shared definition.

choices.text: All of them point at the data model, which solves each one
choices.why: The model answers size. It does nothing for many writers, rules, history or distribution.

prompt: Match each situation to what the job needs, by the lesson's table.
hint: Writing, reading, size, or nothing at all.

pairs.left: Two people must enter sales into the same file at once
The same report goes out by e-mail every week to readers
A file is nearing the last row of a sheet
One analyst, one question for today, a few thousand rows

right_distractors: A second copy of the workbook

prompt: Café Serra opens a second shop whose counter enters sales all day, while the owner keeps adding wholesale orders. What does that call for first?
hint: Is the new problem about writing or about reading?

choices.text: A BI platform, so the dashboard can be published
choices.why: Nobody new is reading. Two places writing at once is a database's job.

choices.text: A database that both can write to at the same time
choices.why: Right. Many writers is the first signal in the table that points there.

choices.text: Saving the workbook as `.xlsx` to get more rows
choices.why: It already has the current grid. Rows were never the problem.

choices.text: A second `Calc` sheet for the new shop's pivot tables
choices.why: That organises reading. The trouble is two people writing the same records.

prompt: The records move from the workbook into a database. What happens to the pivot tables, measures and dashboard of lessons 15 to 17?
hint: Which job leaves the workbook, and which stays?

choices.text: They keep working, through Power Query and the model
choices.why: Right. What leaves is holding the records; asking questions of them can stay in Excel.

choices.text: They have to be rebuilt as SQL queries
choices.why: SQL can answer the same questions, but nothing forces the move. Power Query reads a database.

choices.text: They stop refreshing, since a data model cannot read from a database
choices.why: A database is one of the sources Power Query connects to, as lesson 13 described.

choices.text: They move into the database with the records
choices.why: A database holds tables. The pivots and the dashboard stay where the questions are asked.

prompt: Which of these is a job the lesson would leave in Excel exactly as it is?
hint: Look for no many writers, no many readers, no rule that must hold.

choices.text: Five people entering orders at once into one shared file
choices.why: Many writers is a database's job, co-authoring or not.

choices.text: A weekly report e-mailed to forty people who only read it
choices.why: That is distribution, and it points at a BI platform.

choices.text: A price list that the web shop's system must update directly
choices.why: Another system writing the data is integration, a database's job.

choices.text: One analyst's question for today, on a small file
choices.why: Right. Moving it would only add cost.

prompt: On your workbook, what does `=SUMIFS(Sales[Revenue], Sales[Channel], "Wholesale")` return?
hint: The first row of the SQL query's result.

prompt: Which lessons of this course carry over most directly to Power BI, in `analytics-bi`?
hint: Power BI is built from the same parts.

choices.text: Lessons 2 to 6: references, logic, lookups, conditional totals and text
choices.why: Those are worksheet formulas. Power BI has no cells to put them in.

choices.text: Lessons 8 and 9: validation and conditional formatting
choices.why: Both belong to cells on a sheet, which Power BI does not have.

choices.text: Lessons 13 to 16: Power Query, the data model and DAX
choices.why: Right. The same M language, the same kind of model, and DAX written the same way.

choices.text: Lessons 1 and 18: the shape of the data and the limits
choices.why: Both are worth carrying anywhere, but they are ideas, not the parts Power BI is built from.

prompt: In `sql-databases`, what takes the place of lesson 8's validation, which a paste can get round?
hint: Something the database checks, not something it suggests.

choices.text: Conditional formatting rules stored in the database
choices.why: Formatting colours a value; it never refuses one.

choices.text: Data types and constraints, checked on every row that arrives
choices.why: Right. Its lesson 3, and nothing gets round them.

choices.text: An input message shown before each entry
choices.why: A message asks politely. A constraint refuses.

choices.text: A drop-down list for every column
choices.why: A list helps a person type. It does not stop a program or a paste.

prompt: Why does the lesson suggest taking `statistics` before the other two courses?
hint: What does a dashboard of averages and changes depend on?

choices.text: Averages and changes need a sense of what they hide
choices.why: Right. Knowing when a change is noise is what makes a Revenue YoY % worth reading.

choices.text: It teaches the SQL that `sql-databases` assumes from its first lesson
choices.why: SQL is `sql-databases`' own subject, from its first lesson.

choices.text: Power BI cannot be installed without having finished it first
choices.why: No course is a requirement for installing software. The reason is about reading numbers well.

choices.text: It explains the data model's memory limits
choices.why: Those are this lesson's subject. Statistics is about what numbers mean.

prompt: Put these courses in their order in the BI track, starting from this one.
hint: Positions 3 to 8.
trap: Putting analytics-bi straight after this course skips the database and the statistics it rests on.

prompt: You double-click a CSV export, click past a warning, and the sheet looks full and clean. What do you check first?
hint: A full-looking sheet is exactly what the edge produces.

choices.text: Whether the sheet is protected
choices.why: Protection affects typing, not loading.

choices.text: Whether co-authoring is switched on for the file
choices.why: Co-authoring has nothing to do with how many lines arrive.

choices.text: Whether the dates arrived as text, as lesson 6 warned they can
choices.why: Worth checking afterwards, but dates as text do not raise a loading warning.

choices.text: Whether the file has more lines than the sheet has rows
choices.why: Right. Count the rows that arrived against the lines in the file, as lesson 1 counted after a paste.

prompt: Which of these are signals for a BI platform rather than a database? Choose all that apply.
hint: Reading, not writing.

choices.text: The same report is e-mailed every week to people who only read it
choices.why: Right. Distribution: one published copy instead of a file per inbox.

choices.text: Two people need to enter sales at the same time
choices.why: That is writing, a database's job.

choices.text: One KPI is defined in three workbooks and gives three answers
choices.why: Right. A shared model defines it once for everybody.

choices.text: A rule must hold even for data that is pasted in
choices.why: That is a constraint, a database's job.

choices.text: Refreshing and sending the report is somebody's Monday morning
choices.why: Right. A schedule does it instead.
